t: Introduction: commission examination and quality of medical care
n: This session is devoted to commission examination and the quality of medical care. In professional offences of medical workers the main task of commission forensic medical examination is to assess the quality of medical care given to the patient. Such an examination is ordered when, in an investigation or court hearing, questions arise that require special medical knowledge. In today's session we shall study the defect in medical care, abbreviated DMC, its types, causes, influence on outcome and the assessment algorithm.

First let us define three basic concepts. A patient is a person who has sought medical care, regardless of whether there is disease. Quality of medical care is the set of features showing the conformity of care to modern science and standards. A medical standard is an ordered sequence of diagnostic and treatment measures in volume and character. That is, a patient is a person who has sought care, quality of care is the features of conformity to standards, and a standard is a sequence of measures.

t: Role of standards in the examination
n: We draw attention to the role of standards in the examination. Standards are necessary for determining the type and volume of care. They are important in the examination in deciding the correctness, justification, completeness and timeliness of care. Thus a standard serves as a basis in assessing care in four respects: correctness, justification, completeness and timeliness.

t: Standard and the doctor's creative approach
n: Let us consider the relation between the standard and the doctor's creative approach. Standardisation removes methodological disparities and inconsistencies in staff actions and achieves consistency. But a standard must not push the medical worker towards mechanical observance of requirements. In each case the doctor should approach creatively and be able, on the basis of evidence-based medicine, to make additions and changes to the general standards. This means that a standard does not restrict the doctor's thinking, but gives a consistent basis.

Now the concept of evidence-based medicine. The term "evidence-based medicine" was proposed in the early 1990s by Canadian scientists of McMaster University. D. Sackett in his 1996 definition expressed it thus: the conscientious, reliable and informed choice of the best results of clinical practice for treating a specific patient. Evidence-based medicine combines the doctor's individual experience with the best systematised independent clinical research.

Application of the principles of evidence-based medicine improves the quality of care in safety, effectiveness and cost. The World Health Organization, that is, WHO, prepared a methodology for developing clinical guidelines in 2002. In the same year the Guidelines International Network, abbreviated GIN, was founded. Its task is to create guidelines in international cooperation.

The concept of DMC. A defect in medical care is not a legal concept. In the broad sense it is failure to meet, or improper meeting of, a generally accepted rule, instruction, guideline or regulation, which has led or could lead to an adverse outcome. From the standpoint of criminal law only defects that caused an adverse outcome in a causal connection are taken into account. Remember: the concept in the broad sense and the view of criminal law are not the same.

t: Why a classification of DMC is needed
n: Why is a classification of DMC needed? The classification provides for determining the essence of the defect, its cause and the degree of its influence on the outcome of the disease or injury. It is important both in commission examination and in checks by institution, association and insurance commissions. The classification ensures consistency in the work of commissions and removes contradictions.

t: Four groups of defects by essence
n: By essence, defects are divided into four groups. By the essence of a defect is meant the content of the shortcoming permitted. Groups: diagnostic, treatment, preventive and other defects. In diagnosis, late diagnosis is given as an example; in treatment, wrong use of a drug; in prevention, violation of sanitary rules; and in other defects, an error in record keeping.

Defects of diagnosis make up the diagnostic group. The first is failure to identify the main disease or injury, or its complication. The second is failure to identify an important concomitant disease. The third is late diagnosis and other defects of diagnosis. That is, the main disease, the concomitant disease and delay of diagnosis require particular attention.

Defects of treatment. These include late hospitalisation and shortcomings in surgical treatment. Also in this group are errors in prescribing and carrying out medical procedures and irrational management of labour. In addition, incorrect use of drugs and other defects of treatment.

Preventive and other defects. Defects of prevention: violation of established sanitary norms and rules and shortcomings of immunoprophylaxis. The fourth group in the text is called other defects of treatment: it includes violation of transport rules and shortcomings of dispensary follow-up. Errors in keeping medical documents also belong to this group.

t: Case analysis: determine the defect group
n: Let us consider a case analysis. After a road traffic accident the patient was found to have fractures of the skull bones, ruptures of internal organs and other severe injuries. On the body a large tear of the mesentery of the small intestine was found, but the doctor did not identify it. Question: to which group does this defect belong and how is it connected with death? First determine the group yourself.

We turn to the classification of DMC by place. By the place of the defect, three groups are distinguished: the prehospital stage, the hospital stage and other institutions. The prehospital stage includes the polyclinic and rural post. The hospital stage includes the district and city hospital. Other institutions include the sanatorium and children's home.

The prehospital stage includes rural doctors' posts, polyclinics, diagnostic centres, ambulance medical care and military infirmaries. The hospital stage includes central district and city hospitals, including those with maternity departments, multi-profile centres and clinical hospitals. This stage also includes emergency care structures, medico-sanitary units and military hospitals.

t: The third group and establishing causes
n: The third group consists of sanatorium-resort institutions, children's homes, inpatient care at home, the blood transfusion service, the MLEC and the non-state system. Establishing causes is important for legal assessment and for measures to eliminate them in future. In accordance with law, the examination conclusion may state the causes of the offence and recommendations for eliminating them.

Causes of DMC. These are the circumstances that produced the defect, and they are conventionally divided into three groups: subjective, organisational and objective causes. Subjective causes include inattention and lack of qualification. Organisational causes include absence of means and shortcomings of organisation. Objective causes include late presentation and atypical course.

Let us distinguish the three groups in detail. Subjective causes: inattentive attitude to the patient and lack of qualification; usually offences committed deliberately or through negligence. Organisational causes: absence of means of diagnosis and treatment, shortcomings in organising the process, lack of consistency. Objective causes: late presentation, atypical course of the disease, severity of the patient's condition and short stay in the institution. Remember: assigning a cause to a group also differs by whether it depends on the doctor himself or not.

Quick question: find the cause. Absence of means of diagnosis and treatment belongs to the group of organisational causes. A patient's late presentation to hospital is regarded as an objective cause. Keep these two examples in mind.

t: Influence on outcome and causal connection
n: Influence on outcome and causal connection. In criminal law the existence of an outcome as a result of the defect is very important, so the influence on outcome is studied separately. A DMC may prolong the duration of treatment, affect disability or death; sometimes it does not affect the outcome at all. Only a direct causal connection serves as a basis for holding the doctor liable.

Now the "defensive attitude of the doctor". The risk of an adverse outcome sometimes prompts the doctor to carry out medical procedures in minimum volume, which is the "defensive attitude". In foreign literature it is called "defensive medicine". It is hard to identify: medical documents and materials on the subjective side of the offence are studied.

Manifestations of the defensive attitude. The first is refusal of a surgical operation or choice of a simpler type, and also prolonging preparation for the operation. The second is unjustified refusal of complex invasive diagnostic methods. The third is arranging unnecessary consultations, consilia and examinations, and referring the patient to other institutions.

The assessment algorithm consists of three stages. The algorithm requires that analysis of the DMC be conducted in a definite sequence. The first stage is the patient's pathology. The second stage is assessment of the doctor's actions. The third stage is the causal connection between action and outcome. It is important not to break this order.

At stage 1 the aetiology, pathogenesis, frequency, timing, speed and severity of the pathology are studied. Conditionality: formal conditions are distinguished, that is, document, instruction, order, and actual conditions, that is, the doctor's capabilities. Justification: complaints, clinical signs, the pattern of complications and probable consequences of procedures are studied.

Criteria for assessing actions. Besides conditionality and justification there are three more criteria. Timeliness: urgent, prompt and elective actions; this criterion applies to prevention as well. Technique of execution: the expert must know the technical methods of the procedure. Completeness: the volume carried out is compared with the volume that could have been carried out.

t: Three variants of influence on outcome
n: There are three variants of influence on the outcome. First: the pathology developed naturally, the DMC did not affect it, no causal connection. Second: the DMC worsened the condition, created a predisposition, an indirect connection. Third: the DMC led to a new pathological process, and here the connection is of 3 kinds, direct or indirect.

t: Case analysis: shortcoming in record keeping
n: Case analysis: shortcoming in record keeping. Through the doctor's inattention a shortcoming was permitted in keeping the case history. This shortcoming had no effect in any way on the course of the pathological process or on the outcome. Question: is there a causal connection? Answer: no, the outcome is determined by the natural development of the disease.

Indirect connection, that is, the predisposing factor. If the DMC did not bring a new pathology but worsened the condition and accelerated its course, an indirect connection arises. Example: in severe combined injuries a tear of the mesentery of the small intestine was not identified. This defect is not the direct cause of death, but it had a significant influence and created a predisposition.

t: New process: a) ligation of the ureter
n: New process, a) ligation of the ureter. Variant 3a: the main disease did not affect the development of the new process, and there is a direct connection between the DMC and the outcome. Example: in hysterectomy the left ureter was ligated by mistake; this was discovered several weeks later. Hydronephrosis developed and the left kidney was removed. As a result the DMC was the direct cause of disability.

New process, b) retained tampon. Variant 3b: the main pathology is also decisive, so there is only an indirect connection. Example: a laparotomy was performed for injury of the intestine, and at relaparotomy a gauze tampon left in the abdominal cavity was found. In the development of purulent peritonitis the injury of the intestine was decisive, and the defect is connected indirectly.

t: New process: c) wrong blood group
n: New process, c) wrong blood group. Variant 3c: the new process resulting from the DMC aggravated the disease and in the end was decisive, a direct connection. Example: blood was transfused on strict indications, and because of lack of qualification the blood group was determined wrongly. A post-transfusion complication developed and death followed. Thus the DMC is directly connected with death.

Grounds for ordering commission examination. The ground: a ruling of the inquirer, investigator or prosecutor, or a court order. In the descriptive part of the ruling the circumstances of the case are set out, then the type of examination and to whom it is assigned, and in the operative part the questions are stated. The questions must be clear, comprehensible and not go beyond the competence of the commission of experts.

Documents submitted to the commission. The case materials, medical documents and objects needed for examination are submitted to the commission. Carrying out the examination on separate extracts from the case history and certificates is not permitted; the full case history is needed. In addition the reference on the worker held liable and departmental inspections are submitted. In case of death, the conclusion on the body or the pathological anatomical record is needed.

t: Composition of the commission of experts
n: Composition of the commission of experts. Commission examination is carried out only in forensic medical examination bureaux; the commission consists of at least three persons. Heads of the institution where the case under discussion occurred, and persons interested in the result, cannot be members. The leading expert, the rapporteur and the members have equal procedural rights and duties.

Structure of the examination conclusion. The conclusion consists of three parts: introductory, investigative and findings. In the introductory part the date, place, ground, composition, questions and materials are stated. In the investigative part the essence of the case and extracts from medical documents and laboratory data are given. Extracts are written with indication of the sheet of the case materials. In the findings part answers to the questions are given.

Requirements for the findings. The findings consist of answers to the questions and must correspond to the data of the investigative part. They must be objective, scientifically substantiated, unambiguous and clear. There must be no findings that rest only on subjective, presumptive data, or that are incomplete, indefinite or contradictory.

t: Rights of the suspect, accused and the worker
n: Rights of the suspect, accused and the worker. Article 179 of the Code of Criminal Procedure sets out the rights of the suspect, accused and defendant in the ordering and carrying out of an examination. They have the right to know the ruling, to challenge the expert, to put an additional question and to become acquainted with the conclusion. In an assessment examination these rights belong to the medical worker held liable.

t: Evaluation of the conclusion and questioning
n: Evaluation of the conclusion and questioning. Participants cannot be present at the commission's session and at the stage of drawing up the findings. Members of the commission may be questioned only on the existing conclusion, after it has been presented. Under Article 187 of the Code of Criminal Procedure the conclusion is evaluated together with other evidence and has no priority force.

Let us summarise. Complex analysis is necessary for the legal assessment of staff activity. It also serves to develop measures for improving the quality of services. The analysis covers the essence of the defect, its cause, place and influence on the outcome.
